theme: Manna, quail, water from the rock, God provides
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 16:1-18:27. These chapters take Israel from the Red Sea toward Sinai. Read them as three tests: hunger in chapter 16, thirst and war in chapter 17, and leadership in chapter 18. Watch for the way God provides each time.
settingTheScene: Israel is now six weeks out of Egypt, and the food they carried is gone. The wilderness is not a good place to feed millions of people. The next three chapters show what the first stages of life with God are like, and they are not easy. The people grumble. God answers with generosity. This is a school of dependence, and the lesson is that the God who redeemed them is the God who will provide for them every day.
observation: The people complain: “Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full” (16:3).
God says, “Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you” (16:4), and it is to test whether they will walk in his law.
In the morning, there is a fine, flake-like thing on the ground. They say, “What is it?” and Moses answers, “It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat” (16:14-15). They call it manna.
Each person gathers as much as they need, “and whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack” (16:18).
Those who keep it overnight find it full of worms and foul, except on the sixth day, when a double portion is given for the Sabbath (16:19-26).
At Massah and Meribah, the people quarrel with Moses for water. They ask, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (17:7).
God tells Moses to strike the rock at Horeb, and water comes out (17:5-6).
Amalek attacks. Joshua fights, and as long as Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails, with Aaron and Hur holding them up (17:8-13).
Moses builds an altar and calls it “The LORD Is My Banner” (17:15).
Moses’ father-in-law, Jethro, visits, and says, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods” (18:11). He advises Moses to appoint judges to share the work (18:13-27).
interpretation:
The first thing to see is how quickly the people go from song to complaint. It has been less than two months since they sang at the Red Sea. Now they say they wish they had died in Egypt. It is a ridiculous and also very human response. When life is hard, we tend to remember the past through rose-colored glasses. They forget the slavery and remember the meat pots.

God’s response is gracious. He does not strike them down. He gives them bread from heaven. But he adds an important detail: it is a test. “That I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.” The test is about daily dependence. They are to gather only what they need for the day. If they try to store it up, it spoils. The only exception is the sixth day, when they receive a double portion. This teaches them two lessons at once: trust God for tomorrow, and rest on the Sabbath. It also shows the connection between provision and rest, a link between the gift of food and the gift of the Sabbath that anticipates the commandments to come.

Moses later explains the purpose: “Man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3). The manna was a daily reminder that life comes from God’s mouth.

At Massah and Meribah, the question is sharper: “Is the LORD among us or not?” It is the question that haunts the whole wilderness, and God answers it by giving water from the rock. The rock is struck once, and life flows from it.

The battle with Amalek is the first attack on Israel after the exodus, and the posture of Moses is the point. He stands with his hands raised, and when they fall, Israel loses. He needs help. Aaron and Hur support him. It is a picture of intercession, and the picture of a community that holds up its leaders. The victory is the LORD’s, not Joshua’s. That is why Moses names the altar, “The LORD is my banner.”

Jethro’s advice shows that God also works through ordinary wisdom. Moses is wearing himself out, and a foreign priest points out that the work must be shared. It is a reminder that good leadership means delegation and that humility is willing to receive counsel.
connection: Jesus says, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35), and he contrasts himself with the manna: “Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die” (John 6:49-50). Paul says the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Jesus teaches us to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). Hebrews 7:25 says Christ “always lives to make intercession” for his people.
application:
Pray for daily bread, and practice depending on God for each day. Resist the urge to store up anxiety about the future.

When you find yourself asking, “Is the LORD among us or not?”, answer with what you know of him.

Ask who is holding up your hands, and whose hands you could hold up. Make a plan to encourage a pastor or a leader this week.
prayerPrompts: Ask God for your daily bread, and tell him what worries you about tomorrow.
Thank him for Jesus, the bread of life.
Ask him to teach you to depend on him.
